title: The Library Cart
description: Second literary source set for the dedicated full mock.
subject: rla
passage:
Darius had learned to measure mornings by the sounds of the neighborhood library: the click of a latch, the scrape of a cart, and the short pause before the first door opened. On the morning that mattered, a blue index card listing the mis-shelved call numbers was already waiting where it did not belong. Darius noticed it, hesitated, and then remembered the promise made the evening before.

The problem was a cart of returned books had been shelved incorrectly just before Darius was supposed to leave for a music audition. Everyone around Darius seemed to have a simple answer. One person said the schedule mattered most. Another said rules existed precisely for moments when people were tempted to improvise. Darius, however, could see details that neither argument fully captured. The weather had shifted, one message had arrived late, and a person who depended on the plan had no easy alternative.

At first, Darius tried to solve the problem without attracting attention. That only made the situation more complicated. A small delay created another choice, and the easy option became less fair to someone else. Darius studied a blue index card listing the mis-shelved call numbers, not because the object itself could answer anything, but because it represented the responsibility that had been accepted earlier.

Finally, Darius decided to correct the sections most likely to confuse patrons and ask the evening assistant to finish the rest from the card. The decision did not produce instant relief. Someone complained, and for several minutes it looked as if the choice had only replaced one problem with another. Then the practical effect became clear: the highest-use shelves were corrected before the library became busy and Darius still arrived at the audition on time. The people who had argued for the fastest solution grew quieter as they saw what the extra effort had protected.

Later, Darius explained the decision without claiming it had been perfect. The point, Darius said, was that a rule or schedule could guide a person without removing the need to notice who would carry the cost of following it blindly. The admission surprised the others more than a confident defense would have.

On the bus, Darius found the blue card still folded in his pocket and smiled before saving it for the next shift. The familiar sounds of the neighborhood library returned, but Darius heard them differently. They no longer seemed like proof that every day should run exactly the same. They sounded instead like a pattern people maintained together, one careful decision at a time.

The situation also shows why responsibility and judgment cannot be judged from one isolated detail. People in the passage weigh immediate results against longer-term effects, and they revise their choices as new information becomes available.
